citation: crates/muster-core/src/painting.rs and kan card a_2LMRCug0P, which raises the general form of the frozen pane in a_2KHGYMpnK. The measured incident behind it is sixteen minutes of a pane that had stopped updating while `muster window` reported it `idle`, and its bridge and client stayed connected.
why:
A pane can stop painting for reasons Muster cannot name - a wedged bridge, a transport that dropped without closing, a daemon still answering requests while one of its terminals went quiet - and every one of them looks identical from the window: the last screen, still drawn, with every layer below reporting health. This is the net under all of them.

The rule is not silence. An idle agent paints nothing all afternoon and is perfectly healthy, so a watch on quiet alone would accuse most of a window most of the time. What makes silence wrong is that something was asked of the pane and nothing came back: an intent that actually reached it - a keystroke, a paste, a scroll - with no frame after it. The app knows the first half because it is the sender; the bridge knows the second because frames go from its stdout into a surface and never past the app. These cases are the rule that joins them.

Two guards decide whether owing a frame is worth saying anything about, and each is here because the sentence would otherwise be false. A pane nothing is drawing paints nothing and cannot be typed into, so it is never newly accused - though a warning already raised about it stays until something answers it. A daemon that has gone away already says so once, naming the machine, and accusing each of its panes as well is nagging.

`deadline` is in milliseconds and is named by every case rather than assumed, so these read as rules about a number rather than facts about one constant. The shipped default is 10s, chosen by the false alarm rather than by the healthy case: a working pane answers a keystroke in milliseconds, so what sets the floor is the longest an honest pane can paint nothing after input, which is a program that turned echo off and is waiting for a password.

`steps` run in order against one clock that only `tick` moves, and every step is followed by a reconcile - which is what the thread holding the real clock does, since every one of these facts knocks on it. `raised` and `cleared` accumulate over all of them. A raise is spelled as its problem key, and a clear as its key and `because`: `painted`, `closed`, `daemon_away` or `off`. The run log carries that word, and it is the only thing that tells a pane that painted from one whose warning went for another reason (kan a_2LWqtPd8E).

cases.name: a pane that answers what reached it says nothing
cases.why: The overwhelmingly common case and the one that has to stay silent: something is typed, the pane paints, and nobody hears about it however long the pane is quiet afterwards. The long tick at the end is an idle agent, which is most panes most of the time - and a watch that accused one would be unusable rather than merely noisy.

cases.name: a pane that answers nothing says so once the deadline passes
cases.why: The measured failure. Input reached the pane, no frame followed, and every layer below goes on reporting health - so this sentence is the only thing in the window that disagrees with a pane that looks fine. Said once rather than on every reading: the watch asks repeatedly about a condition that stays true, and a raise per reading would republish the roster and reopen a sidebar somebody just closed for as long as the pane stayed quiet. A reattach is offered beside it, since the bridge it replaces is the one this window is running for a pane it is showing.

cases.name: and takes it back the moment the pane paints
cases.why: A problem is a condition rather than a message, so the pane painting again is what ends it - and watching the row disappear is the confirmation that whatever was wrong is over. Without this the window would accumulate a permanent accusation against a pane that recovered on its own, which is the common ending: a transport comes back, a bridge is replaced, the daemon gets round to it.

cases.name: the clock runs from the first unanswered keystroke, not the last
cases.why: What somebody does to a pane that has frozen is type into it again, and again. A clock restarted by each keystroke is a deadline that is never reached, so the pane most likely to be frozen would be the one this never reports - and holding a key down would guarantee it. The first thing it did not answer is when it stopped answering.

cases.name: a pane nothing is drawing is not accused, and is not accused for the silence that followed
cases.why: The same guard the typeable watch runs under, and the same reason: a pane the window is not drawing has had its surface thrown away, so nothing paints it and nothing can be typed into it. What it owed when it left the screen it owes nobody. Three false alarms at a time on every launch onto a zoomed tab is where this was noticed for the other watch; here it would be a row about a pane somebody cannot even look at.

cases.name: a warning somebody looked away from is still raised when they look back, until the pane paints
cases.why: The accusation was true when it was made, and looking away does not make it untrue. A pane whose bridge had wedged cleared its warning the moment somebody switched tabs and back, and stayed frozen for three more minutes with nobody told - the clear was the same one a real frame produces, so the roster could not say whether the agent came back or the person had only stopped watching (kan a_2LWqtPd8E). What a pane nobody is drawing must not get is a new accusation, which the case above keeps; one already made waits for a frame, the pane closing, or its machine going away.

cases.name: a warning on a machine that then goes away is taken back, and says that is why
cases.why: The machine's own problem names the cause once, and eight panes each saying they stopped painting beside it is the nagging keying a problem by its condition exists to end. The clear says the daemon went away, so the run log does not read as those panes having painted.

cases.name: a pane on a machine that has gone away is not accused for it
cases.why: A daemon that stops answering takes every one of its panes' frames with it, and the window already says so once, naming the machine and saying it may come back. Eight more rows saying each pane stopped painting would bury the one row that names the cause. When the machine comes back the panes are asked again, and one that is still silent then is silent on its own account.

cases.name: a pane that closes takes its problem with it
cases.why: A problem outliving its pane is a row in the roster naming something nobody can look at - and the pane most likely to be closed is the one that had stopped painting, so this is the ordinary ending rather than an edge of one.

cases.name: one frozen pane is named, and the ones beside it are left alone
cases.why: The shape of the condition, and why the key is per pane rather than per window. Fifteen agents with one frozen is the case worth reporting precisely; a window-wide answer would either accuse fourteen working panes or say nothing while one of them sat dead on screen.

cases.name: a deadline of zero switches the watch off
cases.why: The honest answer for a run with no frames to wait for, and the same knob the typeable watch carries. A watch that cannot be switched off is one that has to be right everywhere before it can ship anywhere.
